source.title: Learning Through Noise: Why Subliminal Learning Works and When It Fails
source.authors: Vincent C. Brockers; R. D. Ventzke; Valentin Neuhaus; Belén Hidalgo-Ogalde; V. Priesemann

record.tranche_reason: The paper tests subliminal transfer in a controlled split-head MNIST setting rather than reproducing the original LLM trait-transfer procedure. Its results directly test whether shared initialization is necessary and examine conditions and mechanisms for transfer.
record.gate_note: The paper studies MNIST classification transfer through auxiliary outputs, not acquisition of a favourite-animal or misalignment trait in an LLM. Rows therefore concern versions B and D: whether transfer requires shared initialization and the role of compatible output heads. The paper's summaries of other studies are not recorded as results. Most plotted outcomes are described qualitatively, so figure-only values are recorded as such.
record.test_reason: In the original's MNIST auxiliary-logit setting, the paper tests and explicitly rejects the shared-initialization explanation. It shows that transfer survives randomized hidden layers and architecture changes when output heads are shared, and that it fails through head incompatibility or drift. This is a specific argument that versions B and D need restating, so T5 rather than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. To add: all evidence comes from MNIST/EMNIST MLPs and CNNs. The authors only conjecture that the vocabulary/unembedding layer plays the head role in LLMs, and they say cross-tokenizer transfer remains open.
record.recipe_differences: The original work transfers LLM traits through filtered, semantically unrelated text outputs. This paper uses a controlled MNIST teacher–student setup with separate class and auxiliary heads, random-noise inputs, and auxiliary-logit matching; it evaluates classification accuracy rather than trait preference.
record.method_sensitivity: Transfer varies with hidden-layer reinitialization, auxiliary-head and class-head compatibility, student architecture and capacity, auxiliary-head size, noise samples per epoch, head perturbation strength, and latent dimension.
record.problems: The evidence is from a controlled MNIST split-head setting, not LLM trait transmission. Most plotted conditions are described without extractable numeric values in the text provided. Main-text means use 20 seeds.
record.rows_left_out: Not all plotted results are separately rowed. Omitted results include the width sweep in Figure 3a, EMNIST class-count results in Figure 3c, auxiliary-head similarity measures in Figures 5 and 6, and auxiliary-head fixed-weight compensation sweeps in Figure 11; they were left out because they are additional capacity, task-complexity, or head-alignment measures beyond the rows needed for versions B and D.

untested.parts: No LLM, and no behavioural trait transmitted via filtered numbers, code or maths. The MNIST task transfer is an analogue only.
LLMs from different base families or with different tokenizers or unembeddings. The case of different hidden layers plus different output heads is predicted by theory but not shown as a row.
LoRA ranks, full versus LoRA fine-tuning in LLMs, and shifted evaluation prompts are not tested.

missing.what: Teacher–student hidden-layer update cosine similarity under aux-head perturbation versus the theoretical bound. This is a direct test of the gradient-alignment mechanism. The fit is good for layer 1, but layer 2 breaks away faster than predicted.

record.verdict_notes: This setting extends the original paper's own MNIST proof of concept rather than its LLM experiments. The B challenge therefore holds only for small classifiers with shared output heads, a condition that partly resembles a shared base. Most rows are figure-only and qualitative; numeric values exist only for R10, R11 and R18.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test acquisition of a teacher's behavioural trait from semantically unrelated, reference-filtered numbers, code, or maths outputs.
Tests independently randomized hidden layers and an MLP-to-CNN student when output heads are compatible; does not test unrelated LLM base families or incompatible tokenizers.
Does not test transmission of misalignment or other alignment-relevant traits.

Tests output-head compatibility and representation transfer in a split-head MLP setting; does not test LLM token entanglement, divergence tokens, steering-vector mechanisms, or the original gradient argument in LLMs.
Does not test LoRA ranks or evaluation prompts different from training. It uses full-network training in its controlled setup, but does not test the claim's LLM robustness conditions.
No prompt-only linked-token intervention is tested.

relationships.reason: Transfer re-emerges for large m with randomized hidden layers (R2–R4) and persists across depth and CNN changes (R7–R9). The randomized-feature student matches the teacher, 0.968 vs 0.969 (R18).

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.condition: MNIST split-head MLP with shared aux and class heads, but independently initialized hidden layers, different depth, or an MLP-to-CNN student
source_check.reason: B predicts failure across different bases. Here transfer persists above chance with randomized hidden layers, depth changes and a CNN student (stated explicitly), and R18 matches the teacher (0.96820 vs 0.96860). R7-R9 are partial in magnitude but still not failures. The fully different case (heads also differ) is untested and predicted by theory to fail (A.3.5), and this group excludes it.

relationships.condition: Shared-initialization gradient argument as the mechanism
relationships.reason: Transfer occurs without shared hidden-layer initialization when heads are compatible (R2–R4, R7–R9, R18), so the shared-init gradient theorem is not a necessary condition.
relationships.display_finding: Transfer occurred without shared hidden-layer initialization when the heads were compatible. So the shared-initialization gradient theorem is not a necessary condition.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Shared-initialization gradient argument as the mechanism
source_check.reason: The shared-init account is shown sufficient but not necessary: transfer occurs with randomized hidden layers when heads are compatible. Shared init also isn't sufficient at large d (R14). That qualifies the account rather than refuting it.

relationships.condition: Output-head compatibility as the carrier, with shared hidden initialization
relationships.reason: Transfer drops or vanishes under: randomized class head (chance, R6), randomized aux head (R5), head perturbations (R12, R13), and aux-head drift at high d (R15, R16).
relationships.display_finding: A randomized class head brought transfer down to chance. A randomized auxiliary head, head perturbations, and auxiliary-head drift at high dimension each made transfer drop or vanish.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Output-head compatibility as the carrier, with shared hidden initialization
source_check.reason: With shared hidden init, transfer is severely disrupted by a random aux head (R5), sits at chance with a random class head (R6), and falls with head perturbations (R12, R13). Freezing heads identifies aux-head drift as the high-d failure (R15, R16).

relationships.condition: Limited auxiliary signal or very high latent dimension
relationships.reason: With m=1, accuracy peaks near 0.83 (R10); with N=10^3 it plateaus near 0.29 (R11). Transfer collapses at large d even with shared init (R14) and residually with both heads frozen (R17).
relationships.display_finding: With m=1, accuracy peaked near 0.83, and with N=10^3 it plateaued near 0.29. Transfer collapsed at large d even with shared initialization, and was only residual with both heads frozen.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Limited auxiliary signal or very high latent dimension
source_check.reason: Under shared init, transfer is bounded: m=1 peaks at 0.829 (R10) and N=10^3 plateaus at 0.291 (R11). It collapses at large d (R14), with a residual drop even when both heads are frozen (R17).

relation.reason: It runs its own MNIST split-head experiments on whether transfer needs shared initialization, and on what gates it.

tranche.reason: The paper explicitly argues that the shared-initialization explanation (and the same-base requirement) needs restating: 'a closely matched initialization is not necessary'. Its own results back this (R2-R4, R7-R9, R18).

source_check.notes: R7-R9 are likely partial, not observed: the theory (A.3.4 fn 6, A.3.5) says shared-heads-only transfer is strongly reduced, and Fig 3b's axis appears to run 0-0.4. The case where hidden layers and heads both differ is theory-only, predicted to fail (A.3.5), which fits B for fully different bases. The R18 near-teacher result is an optimal-condition run (m=500, N=10^6, frozen heads). All evidence is from MNIST/EMNIST MLPs and CNNs; the LLM mapping is conjecture.

statements.correction: R18: Table 3/4 optimal condition, m=500, N=10^6, student feature layers random, shared frozen heads; student 0.96820 [0.96769, 0.96870] vs teacher 0.96860.
statements.problem: Minor: R18 is an optimal-condition run (m=500, N=10^6, teacher class head and student aux head frozen), and the statement does not say so.
Makes no specific claim about this study; the counts can't be checked from this text.

statements.correction: R5: random student aux head (shared hidden init) severely disrupts transfer. R6: random class head keeps accuracy at chance for all m. Separately, randomized hidden layers still transfer for large m (R2-R4, R18).
statements.problem: The visible text is truncated and never mentions 2605.23645, though it cites R5 and R6. This study's main result is that shared hidden-layer init is not necessary, so it does not simply reproduce the shared-init account.

statements.correction: R2-R4: transfer re-emerges for sufficiently large m. R7-R9: students with one fewer or one more hidden layer and an MLP-to-CNN student, sharing only the heads. m=1 peak 0.829 ± 0.024; N=10^3 plateau 0.291 ± 0.044; 20 seeds.
statements.problem: The conditions say two-hidden-layer MLP, but cited R7-R9 use 1- or 3-hidden-layer MLP students and a CNN student (Perlin noise, 3-hidden-layer MLP teacher). Re-emergence also needs sufficiently large m.
Minor wording: 'reinitialises only the hidden layers' applies to R2-R4. R6 reinitialises only the class head, with hidden layers shared.
No claim about this study in the visible text. It is not cited next to 'gradient theorem reproduced and extended in toy models', although it limits that account.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Randomized hidden layers and altered student architectures with compatible output heads
reader_labels.reason: Transfer persists after hidden-layer reinitialization and across depth and MLP-to-CNN changes (R2-R4, R7-R9); the randomly initialized-feature student also reaches teacher-level accuracy in a favorable regime (R18).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: High-dimensional latent representations, even with shared initialization
reader_labels.reason: Student accuracy eventually collapses as latent dimension grows, despite shared initialization (R14).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Compatible output heads and controlled MNIST noise-distillation settings
reader_labels.reason: Hidden-layer changes can preserve transfer when heads are compatible, while randomized class-head initialization leaves performance at chance and head perturbations reduce accuracy (R2-R9, R12-R13, R18).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Restricted auxiliary signal or very high latent dimension
reader_labels.reason: Transfer saturates with limited noise samples or auxiliary capacity, head perturbations weaken it, and high-dimensional training can break it through head drift (R10-R17).
